utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we begin today, Mr. Robinson, as regards the request for presence of counsel to witness General Krstic in which the accused requested that Mr. Visnjic be present in court during the testimony of the witness, the Office of the Prosecutor informed that it does not oppose the request. The Chamber has no issue with the witness's attorney Mr. Visnjic being present in the courtroom during the testimony and therefore grants the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton. Please continue. Just a second. I would ask the registrar to -- to inform the witness and the attorney accordingly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, we left off yesterday discussing the incident of 7 April 1995, and I want to continue with that today, and just want to begin by reminding you a little bit of what you said yesterday. Yesterday, I asked you whether the air-bomb fired on Hrasnica on 7 April 1995 was fired to neutralise a mortar, and then you said, "Not mortar but mortars and there were four of them." And that's at transcript page 33162. And then I asked you where they were, and you said they were in open areas that could be described as parks or locations where there were no buildings, but then you said they were next to buildings, and that's at 33163. So I'm wondering what location exactly in Hrasnica are you describing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope that there's nothing unclear about it. Therefore, mortars bases would be placed on a turf, on grass, where you can put one. You cannot place a mortar on asphalt or concrete. Of course, there were edifices or facilities that today some distance apart. Well, since Hrasnica is a settlement, this implies that there are buildings there, but in the locality where the mortars were stationed, there were no buildings except that in the surrounding area there were buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, it's the case, isn't it, that you actually can't tell us what location the mortars you say this bomb was fired to neutralise were at? You can't tell us what location you mean to describe.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see how it can't be told. If you spot a target that you should fire at, then you act against that target. I can tell you that we fired at mortars, at those mortars.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was where exactly in Hrasnica they were. Do you know or don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know they were in a park, an area resembling a park.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yesterday, General, you said because you couldn't see Hrasnica from Ilidza, in order to have confirmation of what was actually happening there and whether that corresponded to what the commander, the Ilidza Brigade commander, was saying, "There was an area called Siljak, and it was above Ilidza, and these are already the slopes of Mount Igman, and that's from where we could see the force that was inside and the assets, how they were deployed." And that's at transcript 33160 to 33161. So just to clarify that, is it correct that you personally went to Siljak to verify the location of the mortars we're talking about or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The explanation I gave yesterday served the purpose to confirm that I, apart from my obligation to respect and accept the statements and assessments and information available to the brigade commander, and apart from his insistence that fire be opened at those targets so that fire could be curbed being opened at his positions, to personally convince myself, together with brigade commander we jointly found a spot from which we could observe the facts on the ground so that they had find a spot for me from where I could observe the Hrasnica location.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I take it your answer is yes, you personally, together with the brigade commander, went to Siljak, and you saw this mortar battery that you've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, a battery of mortars is six. Now, this was a smaller unit. There were four mortars. Yes, I did see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you then -- and it was -- it was only on witnessing outgoing fire from this mortar battery -- sorry, these four mortars that you gave the final order to launch the air-bomb; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I did not have to see mortars firing. It was enough for me to see the mortars in their defensive deployment. It was by chance that I saw them firing, so I could see for myself that they were there and that they were opening fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your subordinates knew what they were firing at. You all agreed that the target was these four mortars in Hrasnica that had been firing on Ilidza; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me, General, that generally speaking, if the mission -- if -- if your soldiers' mission is to neutralise outgoing fire, the time between you giving the final order to launch and the actual launch of the air-bomb should be rather brief?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's relative. It doesn't have to be brief. I agreed with the commander this proposal for that bomb to be launched. There was confirmation and proof that his previous requests were founded. There's justification that there is a target. In such a situation, he must observe all other regulations concerning the use of air-bombs, which was far more rigorous and precise demanding so that air-bombs would not be used if all security and safety measures are not put in place not to jeopardise civilian population. So that period from the moment when I agreed to launch doesn't have to be brief. Of course, he needed my consent so that he could choose the right moment to carry out that launch. What I said does not mean automatically that after I gave my consent that it would be immediately carried through or maybe at a later point.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So how long did it take the crew in this case to respond to your order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this case we cannot tie that with this situation, as I explained to you what measures had been done preceding to that moment in the preceding days, days preceding the 7th of April. He could have done that on that same day or on subsequent days. We don't have to be bound by any time period, but this is another situation. This is not the same as the situation when the enemy's fire's being opened as preparation for an assault. In such a situation, the crew when reports that they're ready to launch, then the launch will take place at the moment when the threat is highest. In this particular case, there was no launch. There was no attack, no assault to effect a breakthrough, so this launch did not take place simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you actually don't know how long in this particular case it took the crew to respond to your order, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never talked to the crew. My duties concerning this situation did not go through the crew. I issued my consent, and the commander knew at what time they would be ready to launch, knowing his crew and all the circumstances. And by "him," I mean Colonel Radojcic, brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you would agree that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, but I'm telling you that I was -- I shouldn't have known. It was no business of mine to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How long, General, then, did it take the crew in this case to respond to your order to launch the air-bomb on Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to explore -- explain how much time the crew needs for launching an air-bomb. There is a standard number of hours, minutes, for preparations for launch --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. With respect, the question actually was a simple one in response to your assertion that you knew how long in this case it took for the crew to respond to your order to launch the air-bomb. So I simply asked you then, well, how long was it? Are you able to tell us or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a misleading question. The witness stated that he did not command the crew. It wasn't his order to the crew. The crew received their orders from either chief of artillery of the brigade or from the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Irrespective of that statement, I think the general can answer the question whether he knew or how long it took for the crew to respond to the order to launch the air-bomb. Whether he knew or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know that the crew needs certain time to launch. This is a technical matter. I'm cautious not to err in this respect. I reiterate: It depended on at which stage of readiness they were at the moment, had they made certain calculations or not. If they hadn't made calculations to prepare the asset for launching, then they would need one -- one and a quarter, up to two hours to place the air-bomb on the launcher, to make the calculations, and to determine all the other details that are necessary so that they could declare that they were ready to launch. And whoever manipulates an asset, they must say, "I'm ready to fire" or "ready to launch," and from that point onwards the commander who decides or chief of artillery will then utter "Fire," command fire, or use the term "Launch," or "Act." They can choose between those expressions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, General. Now to move on, you witnessed the air-bomb launch from Siljak, I take it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I saw from Siljak was confirmation whether there was a target as claimed by brigade commander, that he had insisted that there were on the preceding days. I wasn't there when the air-bomb was launched. I wasn't there when it was launched. I did not observe it personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, then maybe we can go over back to something you said yesterday. Yesterday, I asked you whether you received information that the mortars were neutralised, and that's at transcript 33163, but you didn't really answer that question. You just said: "As for some more immediate indicators, then I would perhaps receive further such information or data about the situation as it was." So did you receive information then, not having seen the launch, that the mortars were neutralised?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have an impression that either you did not understand me well yesterday or that you are trying to obfuscate something which is clear enough. As I explained yesterday, and what I'm going to say now is what I wanted to say yesterday if I was not clear, and this is it: In the order to the brigade commander, it was said that he should report when he was ready to launch. So an order is issued, and then after that preparations ensue and they can be used on another occasion. The -- this order to report back that he was ready to launch serves the purpose that I can ask him again through such reporting line whether he took into consideration all the other elements or did a change occur in that area in terms of possible movements of civilians or even removal of those mortars or change in their firing position. So that order, "Report back when you're ready," is a military mechanism that the brigade commander was familiar with. It is attached to orders so that the use of air-bomb may be deferred if circumstances changed on the ground in the meantime. He reported back to me that he was ready to launch, and after that he was given consent to do that. I wasn't there when this happened. I was, you know, in a completely different area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. But, General, did you get a report back -- after this substantial asset had been engaged, did you get a report back to the effect that the mortars had been neutralised, the four mortars you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, when an air-bomb impacts, it does not necessarily mean it will neutralise. That would imply that they would be destroyed. The issue of neutralisation or destruction cannot be formulated in -- in terms that it's either or. Maybe some parts or some assets could be damaged, some could be destroyed, some could be left intact. I got the report back that the action was carried out and that the target was hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So what you're saying is you got a report back that the mortars, the four mortars, had been, whatever word you want to use, neutralised, eliminated, damaged, destroyed, hit. You got a report back saying the four mortars had been hit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done through a regular daily combat report sent from brigade commander to me. Each brigade would send their daily combat report to the command of the corps. This would be, of course, processed in the operations room of a corps command room.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, did the report say that the four mortars -- did it say the four mortars had been hit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would know what was said if I had this report in front of me. I probably knew then what exactly stood there. I can't tell you whether it reported back on destruction, on being -- those being hit. There was a prescribed form for such reports. What I got back as a report was that the target was hit after the launch.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did the report mention the mortars?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mortars were the target to be fired at, to be hit. So when they say, "We acted against the target," it would be superfluous to specify. I cannot tell you whether they mentioned mortars or not. I cannot recall exactly the content of that report, but it wasn't necessary for me to hear whether mortars were neutralised or cannon. This was something which does not have to be specified by the reporting person, because they knew what had to be done against that target.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if they had missed the target, your observation being as good as you say it was and your concerns for safety being as paramount as you say they were, that would also have been reported back to you, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was important to me. I maintain that this was important to me. I'm trying to read your question in a different manner. It was important, let it be known, that the plan would be carried out and that civilians be protected. Furthermore, if we know, and that is so, that afterwards those mortars did not fire from those positions later on, this means that they were hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you don't remember receiving any reports to the effect that the mortars hadn't been hit, that the target had been missed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The target was hit. There was a report, a formulation in the report being that they had implemented their mission against the target. In turn it meant that the goal had been achieved, which was the targeting of mortars. He needn't specifically say that the mortars had been hit. It sufficed to include in the report that the target was hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, General, actually your mission was a failure, wasn't it, because the air-bomb landed on a civilian house and completely destroyed two houses?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You use that particular indicator based on someone else's scene of crime investigation. The investigation brought about certain results, whereas the person who engaged the target established something else. I said that it was their goal to prevent any further fire from those mortars and that was met. The mortars were no longer active in that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, you've just agreed that the air-bomb landed on a civilian house. It didn't land on the mortars at all. And your testimony not five minutes ago was to the effect that the mortars had been hit.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if one wants to play with words. The air-bomb need not land straight on top of the mortar to have it hit. If one wants to be literal in terms of whether it landed on top of the mortar or not, then that cannot be interpreted in any other way other than literally. In the immediate vicinity of those mortars there was something else. In any case, from that point on the mortars could no longer engage. It was our calculation or our assessment that even if something else is being struck, it was of greater importance --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpret's note: I presume the witness wanted to say lesser importance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- than neutralising the mortars. Ms. Edgerton, you need to bear in mind the following: Due to the subject discussed here, I received a very long sentence, and it is my understanding that it was the way the Chamber in my case saw things. I do know, however, that it was my view point which guided my activity, was not to act recklessly or undertake preventive measures and that civilians should not be targeted. Such was not my position, and such were not my decisions. I can no longer keep proving things, and I expect that there should be some degree of understanding, that we did not target civilian targets. If it was interpreted as collateral damage, which may occur in exceptional situations, then it can only be used as an indicator that such victims as may occur have to be far less than what is -- than what we try to obtain by protecting ourselves from such fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm going to leave this for a minute, and I just want to underscore something before I move further, General, so that we have no misunderstanding. When I ask you a question I mean to be literal, and perhaps that can guide you in the rest of our time together. I'd like to go to P1201, which is the order that you gave the day before the launch. It's dated the 6th of April, and it's the order to get the launcher ready and pick a target. So I want to point out a few things to you in this document. Now, first at the top of this document it says: "For the past three days, Muslim forces have been attacking the positions of the 2nd Sarajevo Light Brigade, and the attacks are particularly pronounced in the sector of the Famos factory." So you'll notice that so far there's no discussion of attacks -- well, there is discussion of attacks on the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade, especially near the Famos factory. There's no mention of attacks on the territory of the Ilidza Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely right. Whatever is stated in the document was the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay. So then just going on, there's also nothing here that says there have been attacks at the Ilidza area and the entire part of Stojcevci across the basins, the pools, the institute, the spas, and the villas, like you said yesterday in your testimony, and that's at transcript page 33160?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do kindly try to treat my answers the way I provide them. You merely repeated it, and I accept that I stated precisely as you cited it just now. However, one needs to know the following: I said that the commander of the Ilidza Brigade at the time demanded that I come and see for myself the extent of danger posed to the area his forces were defending. Perhaps just one additional piece of information was obtained, and that was that they carried out the same attacks against the 2nd Sarajevo Unit. It was well known what the degree, what the amount of pressure was on the Ilidza Brigade, and it seemed to continue, because they began attacking the 2nd Sarajevo Unit. That was just another reason to add more weight to our assessment before that and to engage -- and to actually use the full potential of the Ilidza Brigade which was under threat, although that is not specified in so many words.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we go further down, this document says to select the most profitable -- pardon me, the highest yielding target in Hrasnica or Sokolovic Kolonija where the greatest casualties and material damage will be inflicted, and it says nothing about neutralising mortars, mortar batteries, mortar fire, or artillery fire, does it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope you know all too well that soldiers have to be rational in their descriptions when drafting orders and their contents. To try and describe things is superfluous for the brigade commander, because he was well aware of the nature of his problem and what kind of fire his units were receiving. Any irrational description of that sort would undervalue his role of commander. He was well aware of his professional duty and knew how to conduct himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is what you're saying that to mention neutralising mortars, mortar batteries, mortar fire, or artillery fire as an objective of this order would be irrational?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it would be just an unnecessary extra, because he was well aware of his problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, if this mission is to neutralise outgoing mortar fire from Hrasnica, it doesn't make sense, does it, General, to give an order that allows the brigade commander to launch an air-bomb into Sokolovic Kolonija, does it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sokolovic Kolonija was drawing even more fire with more threatening assets. Kolonija as a location is much closer to Ilidza. They were under a different kind of threat coming from such forces in Sokolovic Kolonija. Previous reconnaissance and the decision that was agreed upon between Colonel Radojcic the brigade commander and myself resulted in the conclusion that the matter at hand was actually Hrasnica. In this case, as an alternative or something of a similar sort, he didn't have the right to consider Sokolovic Kolonija which at that point posed no threat, although under such circumstances no new orders were required.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll just leave that for the moment and continue still on the subject of targets, because we've talked about Hrasnica in that line and now mentioned Sokolovic Kolonija. You know, General, Colonel Radojcic actually came here to give evidence as a witness for Dr. Karadzic's Defence, and I asked him what the target of this air-bomb launch was when he came here, and he said, "The target of my brigade was only the command post of the 4th and later the 104th Motorised Muslim Brigade," and he said the command post was in the Hrasnica school. And that's at transcript page 31258. And then a few lines later, he changed that to the post office. And then I asked him who made the decision about what the target was, and he said, "I was the one," at 31262. And, General, he never said anything about neutralising mortar fire. So my question is given that you actually couldn't hit a pinpoint target with one of these devices, evidenced by this incident on the 7th of April, General, it's actually possible that no one had a real target in mind other than just the centre of Hrasnica, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. It's not. That kind of attitude and that kind of situation in which one wouldn't consider the choice of target, that simply didn't come about. Colonel Radojcic knows all too well what we tried to determine and what we had agreed upon. Now, what he said may be a result of his faulty memory or something else which guided him in his testimony. I really can't say. But I am aware of the evil that emanated from it, and I know what it is that he was actually trying to gain. I also remember that the evil that he had to face was simply coming from the system of command commanded by Prevljak, who was the brigade commander before he moved on to assume command of the 12th Division. That kind of activity, that kind of behaviour, the Ilidza area was always in a very awkward situation because of the number of forces and the kind of attitude that Mr. Fikret Prevljak had. Colonel Radojcic kept complaining about their behaviour. He simply didn't have to face a rational or well-meaning command of the 104th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just before we leave this subject, I want to go back to some of the things in your evidence yesterday that you agreed with and then ask you a question. You agreed yesterday, at transcript page 33151, line 13, that any effort to avoid firing air-bombs over residential areas was because of the risk they might have landed on those areas. So that's one thing. And then I asked you a document -- about a document, P1310, and that was the document drafted by Colonel Manojlovic which stated that the firing of a modified air-bomb at the opening of the tunnel was aborted because, among other things, your forces were 500 metres away, and you said that was to make absolutely sure that safety is achieved, and that was at 33153. So what that means, General, is that your colonel had decided that the risk that the air-bomb would deviate from its target by 500 metres and hit your own soldiers was big enough that it didn't even justify firing on what you considered to be a military target; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I think one needs to be grateful to Colonel Manojlovic for taking that position and making proposals and suggestions to undertake all possible protective measures. There is never an asset that can be used in a particular situation without a possibility of some unwanted influence or consequence irrespective of what asset or what situation we are talking about. It includes even the most sophisticated and up-to-date combat means programmed by computers. This proposal of his was a measure against us doing that. Perhaps I needn't repeat it all, but the main reason, the main thrust of his reasoning was this: If within the command there are people who had to think carefully about what we were going to do, then it was up to me to take their opinion into consideration. It actually may have involved UNPROFOR, which was some distance away as we mentioned yesterday. Their movement and their engagement in the implementing of tasks, while in all that they were not a static target. Due to their movement which may well take place at the moment of our firing on the tunnel, it is that which prompted him to be even more cautious, and he called on us to give up on using that asset. We did, cancelled it, and I'm grateful to him for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, that caution that we saw in Colonel Manojlovic's document of 26 April is not reflected, is it, General, in the order of the 6th of April that we've been discussing, and that was also drafted by Colonel Manojlovic, the order to select the most profitable target in Hrasnica or Sokolovic Kolonija where the greatest casualties and material damage would be inflicted. The -- that caution that you saw with regard to an order -- an operation that affected your soldiers is not reflected at all in your order of 6th April.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course what you say about this order being mine is correct. You know that the same order was drafted by Mr. Manojlovic. However, that is irrelevant. What is relevant is that Mr. Manojlovic knew everything. He knew how the process of analysing that problem developed between myself and the brigade command. He knew what measures were taken in that process. Thus it was superfluous to deal with what he knew I was aware of and that he didn't need to include such words and sentences and content which would try to educate us as if we were completely ignorant of the situation. He knew that all too well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yesterday, you also acknowledged having given an order, which is P1309, to prepare for the launch of up to six air-bombs simultaneously at a target with the provision for even more to be launched in case they missed. So you acknowledged having given that order, and you explained that order. General, isn't it the case that, in fact, you, Colonel Manojlovic, Colonel Radojcic, all knew that these bombs were inaccurate, had a wide margin of error of hundreds of metres off target, and so long as they didn't pose a risk to your forces, you felt free to launch them into urban centres like Sarajevo, city centre, and civilian areas like the settlement of Hrasnica? And you'll recall when you began your cross-examination yesterday, you described Sarajevo as civilian.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it all. It is all clear to me. This assertion or an indicator of yours of us knowing that the asset was imprecise is something I do not accept. Quite the other way around. We knew and of course we are in a position to know when confirmed by technical experts with sufficient knowledge in situations where they can deal with inaccuracies until they have come up with a reliable asset. I stand by the fact that we knew -- well, perhaps you will not believe me or this may not be taken judicial notice by the Chamber, but I do know that we were at some point in a situation that such bombs achieved more accuracy than, for example, when dropped from aeroplanes. It was actually confirmed that they frequently missed their target if dropped from aeroplanes. And there were no such cases in our situation, in our case. I have to go back and say that we have received confirmation that they can be used. Actually, had there been any doubts, any reservations about that asset, it would never have been used. That is what I state here now. We would never have used the assets if we had known that it could achieve great dispersion or miss the target. Well, it was not our position to use assets in a way so as if to say, "Well, wherever it landed, it's fine." No officer could allow that. "We don't have parameters, but let's go ahead with it in any case," that's simply not true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An intervention for the transcript. What is missing in the transcript is that the witness said that a projectile could "fall short" or "fall over a target" in line 14. The witness said that it was also taken into consideration that that kind of asset would not overshoot or fall short of a target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think we've spent long enough on this area, and I'll move on to a different area, General, and a different part of the city of Sarajevo. In your testimony in chief to Dr. Karadzic, you said at transcript pages 32567 to 32568 that the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were not at Spicasta Stijena. So, General, how many times have you actually visited your forces in that area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions. I can't be specific, five or four times, but at any rate, that kind of number of times. Let me confirm why this was so, why I visited those places several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, with respect, let's -- my question was just about how often you'd been there. So if you want to come back to that with Dr. Karadzic you can. So I'm wondering whether, General, during your visit to the area if you didn't see the Serb flag flying from the flag pole situated on the ridge at Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'd never said that I saw that Serbian flag.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you see it or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we be more specific about the time, the relevant time concerning this question and answer? When?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, Mr. Tom Knustad, a United Nations military observer who was positioned in Sedrenik gave evidence in your own trial, and his evidence was received by this Chamber in P00123, and he -- and that being the transcript of his evidence in General Milosevic's trial, I'll just give you the transcript page there, it's 2030. And he said there that they knew -- his UNMO team knew that Spicasta Stijena was under VRS control because of the Serb flag that had been erected on the ridge. General, did you see the Serb flag on the ridge?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we be given an indication of time? When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's be on the same page. What I can recall from my trial, I know there were photographs of a Bosnia-Herzegovina flag at the Grdonj feature. First I can't recall Mr. Knustad saying that. That's one thing. Secondly, I never paid attention whether there was a flag hoisted or not. I cannot tell you anything about that. Please do not ask me anything about the flag on this occasion, because this is the first time I hear a question about that flag. This is the first time I hear about the existing of a flag. Well, there were -- there was a flag elsewhere at Zlatiste, but not there. It is not known to me. I never paid attention. I never issued an order, nor could I tell you anything about that Serb flag at the Spicasta Stijena. I cannot tell you anything about that really.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So that's fine. Now, you said you had visited your troops in that area four or five times. Now, Mr. Karadzic has actually called two company commanders, two Mrkovici commanders to testify in his Defence case, Sinisa Maksimovic and Blasko Rasevic, and these are two people who served on the line, and both gave evidence that their company held Spicasta Stijena. And battalion commander Slavko Gengo at T 29786, transcript page 29786, also confirmed that Spicasta Stijena was under Bosnian Serb Army control throughout the whole conflict except for one day around the 18th September, 1994. So, General, these three men were your own subordinates, two company commanders and a battalion commander, and they were deployed at that feature, Spicasta Stijena, and gave this evidence under oath. So, General, on their evidence it appears that your assertion is actually not true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we ask for the precise quote of what was said about where the lines were? What did these witnesses say where the lines were in relation to Spicasta Stijena, because what has just been said is not something that they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm happy to provide the page citations, Your Honour. More specifically, Mr. Maksimovic gave evidence that Spicasta Stijena was in his area of responsibility, and that's at D2354, paragraph 9; that Muslim forces took it only once in mid-September 1994. That's at D2354, paragraph 10. And he told this Chamber that the SRK recovered the ridge a couple of days later, and that's at transcript page 23 -- pardon me, 29303. Mr. Rasevic, who was also a company commander at Mrkovici from January 1993 until September 1994, and who was in that area throughout the war gave evidence that from as early as April 1992, Serb forces took up positions from Velika Trdzva [phoen] to Spicasta Stijena, and that was the case throughout his tour as company commander, and to quote from him at D2527, paragraphs 20 and 29, he said, "Our positions included Spicasta Stijena." Would Your Honours like me to somehow be more precise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In -- in -- no, my question is, Your Honours -- pardon me. Would Your Honours like more information in regard to what these witnesses have said in addition to the citations I've provided?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, my question, General, was -- so these three men were your subordinates, two company commanders and a battalion commander, and they were deployed in that area, and they gave this evidence under oath. So my question is: On their evidence, it appears that your assertion is actually untrue, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not untrue. First of all, if we're talking about Maksimovic and him saying that he was at the Velika Trdzva-Spicasta Stijena line, the place Velika Trdzva, as you heard from him and noted it down, is located over 1.500 metres from the area that we're talking about here. Now, that's one thing. So we can only talk about something that refers to Mala Kula, and Mala Kula is a line. It's an area that our forces reached, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps forces reached up to that point. That is the main indicator where they were. From Mala Kula to the positions of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, there is more than 250 metres. This is what I remember and the situation that I was overseeing on several occasions. Once at a given point in particular I was monitoring it, and this is what I want to say before this Trial Chamber. What happened in this initial period of combat was that the forces of the 1st Corps took Mala Kula. They moved our forces and occupied that area. By capturing Mala Kula they also captured the area to the left and to the right of it. Now, this was a situation that jeopardised our defence. We had to pull back, and then we did everything to get those forces out of Mala Kula or from that line to be more precise. So this is an indicator, a parameter, and my recollection, everything that has to do with that area. This Mala Kula and everything is behind Grdonj hill. So the way I remembered it and what I experienced in that area is still fresh because it was a sensitive area for several reasons and represented an important point for the corps force as a whole. We managed to push the -- their forces back. And what I'm ask now is that when these same fighters, when they went back to Kula, why didn't they advance? They said they couldn't advance because their area was already on the edge when the ground already begins to slow. So from Mala Kula up to that edge or the area where the land begins to slope down, I said there was a distance of some 250 metres. So going forward would mean going into their disposition. So I stopped there with my fighters. I said very well. Now you have resolved the problem. We tried to record that for television, but it was very late in the evening hours. I don't know how they broadcast that later, because on the fourth night, Television Sarajevo showed how they had captured this Kula, and then we went for the option to tell them that this has now been returned to us. So my evidence and indicators. While touring that area, nobody -- well, we that couldn't -- didn't call that area where the forces were deployed Spicasta Stijena or any other name, because the term "Spicasta Stijena" is of local origin, and for me who is looking at the situation from a different aspect, I would not use that local name but I would use the topographical names that you could find on a map, and what you can find on the map is the Grdonj feature, 950 metres, the highest point in that area that was held by the forces of the 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And there is a certain plateau which somebody most probably later thought of as Spicasta Stijena. Actually, that plateau was just in line with this Kula that I'm talking about, and then the front proceeded viewing at it from the four directions to the south, towards those -- I assume they had Sedam Suma. I really cannot be specific about that right now, this axis going on towards Hladivode however those features were called. In this case, Spicasta Stijena as some kind of practical feature or facility literally associates -- the name means "peak," "spic," so this area which is isolated and elevated and set apart did not exist in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, but I am not denying that it is a little bit elevated in relation to the other terrain which looks on Sarajevo, but I'm not talking about the edge of this terrain, but I'm talking about a certain depth from the rear because we couldn't reach this edge in view of the fact that the actual edge, the very last angle at which the terrain begins to slope is area that they held. And this is what I know, and I am going back now about the flag, and I really don't know anything much about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There's no need to go back. Thank you, General. So listening to your lengthy explanation, as I told you I want to be literal in my questions, I'm going to read you what battalion commander Gengo said, actually said, about Spicasta Stijena. He was asked at 29786, line 7: "Now I'd like to ask you a few questions, Mr. Gengo, about a location known as Spicasta Stijena. You know this location?" He answered: "Yes." He was asked: "The VRS held it throughout the 1992 to 1995 conflict; is that correct?" He answered: "Yes." Later on he explained that he believed it was on 18 September 1994 it fell under ABiH control for one evening. He was asked: "Now, from Spicasta Stijena you had an excellent view of that part of the city of Sarajevo." He responded: "Only the part known as Sedrenik." And he was asked -- or pardon me. If we go down to transcript page 2987 -- 29787, he explained at line 5: "My three trenches on Spicasta Stijena were under crossfire from the enemy, from Kresa on the right, from Borovo on the left. They were always under crossfire, and I had to dig those three trenches on Spicasta Stijena, and I can show you the how the men who defended their part of the village approached those trenches." So actually your own battalion commander has directly, before this Chamber, contradicted the evidence you've just given, hasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what is contradictory here, what the commander of the battalion was describing. He knew what it was and where it was. As for how you understood what -- where this was, I -- I don't know. Unless he specified that it was along that line that I am talking about, the line of Mala Kula, and that in front of him some 250 metres away and somewhere closer the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army had its positions. Perhaps he wasn't precise and he didn't know that he needed to provide those details to you as well. I'm not denying his story, what he's saying. I am stating what I know about the situation, when I was getting information about it, and the situation in that area which was important to us. It's not unimportant. If you wish, I can remind you, although I'm sure you know that very well, that a witness who was testifying in my case said, "No, no, that was not Spicasta Stijena, that was some kind of valley or gorge through which the Muslim forces were passing," and he said that the local name for that area was Smreka. He said he went to school there, he would pass there, and he never knew of any feature called Spicasta Stijena. I am trying here to say that if it will be taken into account that the term "Spicasta Stijena" as an association to some sort of prominent feature, I would say, is something that is imposed, imposed. It has a different connotation, a different aspect. I must, I must, explain to the Trial Chamber. Such a feature that is prominent, that is at an elevation, it's not usually captured. It's a highly visible firing point. Actually, it can be exposed to enemy fire according to a simple recipe, and nobody would want to expose themselves in that way. Further on, if you're prepared to hear me out, I know that one of the witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you're going to start talking about witnesses in your own trial again, I'd actually ask that we move on. You can talk to Dr. Karadzic in your redirect about witnesses in your own trial. All right? I'd like --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would ask --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Please, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you answered the question, and we can proceed. Ms. Edgerton, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go on to the subject of sniping, and at transcript pages --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honour, I just see it's 10.28, and maybe before going on to this different area -- I'm in Your Honour's hands. It might be an appropriate time for a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we take a break, Mr. Milosevic, so you had your own trial, and then I take it that this -- this issue was one of the issue in your trial as well. Am I correct, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So whatever the name it might have been, you should know the place where -- which was referred to as Spicasta Stijena in your indictment, and I take it that it is your evidence that specific place was not under Serb control. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I understood you correctly. I am saying what was under our control and what the disposition was, what it looked like, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me put my question more directly. This sniping from so-called Spicasta Stijena was included in your indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you understood that what place it was, where it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was that place, that specific point which was called Spicasta Stijena in your indictment was under Serb control during the war? At any time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I understand. I'm not specifying that area, and I don't call it Spicasta Stijena. I am talking about the position and the disposition of the units of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps which, among other things, executed certain kinds of fire whereby I'm not ruling out any kind of action as impossible. Quite the contrary. They did have conditions from that position to execute possible fire, and that possible fire was executed to the degree required for them to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We'll leave it at that, and we'll break for half an hour and resume at 3 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, in your testimony in chief in the context of a discussion about the anti-sniping agreement on 14 August 1994, Dr. Karadzic asked you what the sniping fire from the Serbian side was conditional on, and your answer was: "When their sniping fire stopped, ours stopped as well and there was no further need for further sniper fire." And that's at transcript 32840 to 32841. Do you mean by this to say that sniping by your forces was exclusively military on military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put a very clear question, and I'm prepared to answer. I have to ask the Trial Chamber regarding the previous situation, not the details but its about a request that I have to try to give an explanation. Not about the events but it has to do with my need, and then I will answer this question. I have understood it, and I remember it. Your Honours, I would just kindly ask to express a problem that I have in just a couple of words and to say something further about my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm trying and I want to state here, express here, that I'm not here to defend myself, and any indicator that I state, I would not wish for it to be understood or treated as if I were stating things that were untrue or incorrect. I'm just stating this in order to draw a parallel between the assertions that these gentlemen made in their testimony and some alleged collusion, which is how I'm experiencing it, because my indicators say something else. First of all, it is not my intention to negate the testimony of those who testified here before me, and I would like to note that there is no single event that can be described or confirmed in the same way by two different persons. My views and the way I understood events is one approach, and I just wanted to state that that was my view of things, not any negation of what happened or an attempt to distort events. This is something that is a characteristic of my entire testimony here, and I am obliged by a number of things, including my honour and honesty, to speak the truth, and I would like to thank you for allowing me to say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. I'd like to reiterate here that you are not here to defend yourself but give evidence in the case of Mr. Karadzic. All you have to do is to tell the truth, nothing but the truth, whole truth to the Chamber as far as you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember my question, General, or would you like me to repeat it for you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember it, but I wouldn't mind hearing it again. Could you please put your question again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The question is: Do you mean, did you, in responses to Dr. Karadzic related to the anti-sniping agreement mean to say that sniping by your forces was exclusively military on military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what I wanted to say, and that is what the practice was. In that regard, I hope that I will have the opportunity to tell you something in more detail about the reason for such an assertion or what in essence I want to say with that about the events, the occurrences relating to sniper action. I hope that I will have the opportunity to explain all of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your evidence is that sniping by your forces was exclusively military on military, even though the anti-sniping agreement was initiated, negotiated, signed, and recognised as a measure to protect civilians on both sides against sniping. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was accepted in its entirety. When the use and the fire by snipers ceases, that implies that civilians would be protected as well. If you want to understand me, the motive and taking the position and attempts and trying to get the agreement to hold, I was precise in that way, among other things, because I also felt that my soldiers would be protected from an exceptionally widespread fire of that type by forces of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If sniping is exclusively military on military, then the implication is that there would be no civilian victims. Are you saying that there would be -- there was -- were no civilian victims of sniping in Bosnian-held Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm never going to say that there were no civilian casualties regardless of the type of fire which caused them to be casualties. I hope that you will take that into account. This would make no sense, and it wouldn't be all right to have anybody claim that there were no casualties. Then everything would make absolutely no sense, and then there would be no need for us to speak at all if that was the assertion. This is not what I'm saying. I'm saying that the casualties ought to be respected and that a solution ought to be found so that there are no casualties.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. But what makes no sense then to me, General, is if -- is how your assertion stands in the face of what you said in your testimony in chief to the effect that your forces never targeted civilians.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It stands literally in the way that you're putting it now. It's not a fact that anyone -- it's not something that can be ruled out. There was nobody's accord or approval or secretly even anybody giving a suggestion that fire should be directed at civilians. I would like us to agree on the fact that it's not true that civilians were not exposed to injuries or were not hit, but there was an attempt by us for the whole combat structure and in this case sniper operators to tell them that they must not operate in that way and that it constitutes a harmful situation that brings harm to us ourselves. I don't know how far I would need to go into explanations about how each of those soldiers was aware that it was not his need or his commitment, their personal commitment, to fire at civilians, that there was no advantage to be gain -- gained by that in terms of their own defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps you could repeat your last sentence, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last sentence was that a civilian never attacked a soldier so that a soldier would then be prompted to return fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. But, General, if the fact that sniping -- that civilians in -- the preponderance of victims of sniping in Sarajevo were civilians, that sniping of civilians in Sarajevo continued incessantly for three and a half years in a widespread fashion across the areas of operation of a number of military brigades suggests exactly the opposite, doesn't it, that the sniping of civilians in Sarajevo was a policy, that it was directed, and specifically -- specifically -- and that it specifically targeted the most vulnerable residents of the city?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You've posed several questions. First of all, I don't understand what you mean by saying a series of military brigades. I don't know what you mean by that. A number of military brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, sniping against civilians in Bosnian-held Sarajevo created victims across the breadth of the city, victims exposed to firing positions of any number of brigades of your corps. How can you, in light of that and evidence that we've heard that this continued throughout the duration of the conflict say that no approval was issued to snipe, no suggestion was issued to snipe? In fact, it was a policy that was directed, wasn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a problem for you to stick to what you're saying, but I would like to ask if it's possible when you refer to such events where exactly you have those places or areas from which a number of our brigades opened sniper fire. Could you please be more specific, more precise, and I know why I'm asking you this. Why I'm asking for you to do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it difficult for you to answer my question as to whether sniping against civilians in Sarajevo was a policy, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not difficult for me. That was not difficult for me to say. However, in my attempts to depict and describe this whole situation, your questions went into a direction which precluded my explaining what is really important. My first assertion is that simply we think that the regulations and rules concerning the use of snipers, and I literally mean sniping on the part of individual soldiers who were issued by a sniper rifle, that rules and regulations were carried out and implemented to that extent which was sufficient so that anybody who was in possession of a sniping rifle knew how to conduct themselves. This is one of the considerations that I had no occasion to express so far. Furthermore, the issue of use of snipers was not a centrally governed issue which would allow the use of sniping only if ordered from a certain level. The level of units which is allowed to have snipers deployed, and there is an additional consideration is that we recruited for sniping activities only those personnel who had the mental patience and attributes that would allow them to be effective snipers. That level command was company command. At no point was it allowed that a conduct or an action by personnel that would be their own conduct, of their own will. It was always commanded or ordered.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, General, just before I lose track of what you've said here, you've talked about rules and regulations and direction ensuring that people -- pardon me. I'd like to find the cite. I thought I heard the general referring to people in possession of a sniper rifle knowing how to behave, but what you've -- what you've -- what you've said here is you referred to rules and regulations were carried out and implemented to the extent that it was sufficient that anybody who was in possession of a sniper rifle knew how to conduct themselves. Now, General, this Chamber's received demographic analysis of the number of civilians killed and injured as a result of sniping in Sarajevo between 1992 and 1994, and the number of observed and recorded -- so only those observed and recorded deaths related to sniping was 336. That's even before the period that you assumed command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and a total of 1.789 observed and recorded woundings of civilians in Bosnian-held Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And those numbers, Your Honours, come from P4997 and P4998, page 5 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, the numbers alone I'd suggest to you contradict your assertion that people in possession of sniper rifles knew how to behave themselves. It suggests -- or the number suggests they're conducting themselves in a manner specifically geared to keep the civilian population locked down, fearful, and under pressure. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not the one who could now dispel that assertion, which is a matter of certain formulation, locked down, intimidated, those people, I mean, et cetera. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did not put those people into such a position and exploited that situation in an arrogant way or in a way which would characterise their attitude as arrogant. I neither agree with that nor can I accept it. I do believe that a different approach should be taken to that. But this is not something I can deal with in terms of that assertion. Neither can I comment those figures before I assumed my position. Or later to the -- there's no sense in depriving those figures of any sense. I don't think it would make sense to present things which are not true, and along these lines we should try to find a solution. There is no established situation whereby you could make an assessment that those people could have met their either death or injury under different circumstances, but those matters cannot fit with the conduct of sniper soldiers of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Please do take this in the right way. I reiterate that those soldiers were honourable men and they didn't want to do that. I have a number of other pieces of information I can share with you if the conditions are created that allow me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you saying -- are you saying that Bosnian authorities are responsible for the killing and wounding of civilians by your forces, the civilians in Bosnian-held Sarajevo, because they exploited their situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do not exclude that action from being possible. I do not exclude the responsibility of the forces of the Bosnian Army through carelessness or other means that they may have created victims, so to create an atmosphere of being the endangered party or try to prove that. Why in the data expressed by Mr. Sefer Halilovic, BiH Army commander for a period of time, who stated that citizens, civilians, could not walk down the street due to the activities of our snipers. What prompted him to say that, I don't know, but there are many indicators where things could have unfolded that way and where certain elements of the Muslim forces could have been the causes of such events. Not necessarily soldiers. I have information about certain groups who conducted themselves in that way who created certain circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Putting -- putting whatever Mr. Halilovic might say aside, because he's not come here to give evidence before this Chamber, I'd like to just tell you what somebody else has said about people not being able to walk the streets of Sarajevo. Brigadier-General David Fraser gave evidence here and said that the problem of sniping was so acute in Sarajevo that a specialised task force was established and put in place along Sniper Alley to observe sniping positions, engage snipers who were firing at civilians from those positions, and they put barriers in place to protect civilians from sniper fire in SRK-held territory. General, I put to you based on that that this isn't a question of creating an atmosphere of being endangered. In point of fact, civilians in Sarajevo were under direct and constant threat of snipers operating within your forces.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you persist saying that they could only have been part of our forces. If one retains this assertion that it only pertained to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, it will be a blind alley. This conversation will not go much further because that's the way you put things. I'm trying to provide explanations. I was trying to explain the following: When there is combat, these are not merry situations, of course, and they do not necessarily exclude the possibility of having an impact on people who have nothing to do with the combat itself. There is also another thing that I do not exclude. I do not exclude the possibility that a deranged mind on the Serbian side engaged in such activity. However, it cannot be put under the idea of a policy of people engaging in combat in order to protect their area. They were trying to do sensical things. I'm not certain -- or actually, I do know that many things haven't been cleared up. It is enough, and that is what I'm trying to state here, is this: When there is an attempt of breakthrough one after another and in the end, for example, Spicasta Stijena is the main location from which a force was stopped or -- well, maybe it didn't stop anything, but if they had an intention to break through or occupy an area, and in that context our will prevailed with respect to sniping activity, then the positions were switched or there was a confusion. And the same situation applies to Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you saying that sniping would increase -- sniping against civilians would increase following Bosnian operations to break out of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's the other way around. I'm not saying that. I'm trying to say that a solution was found so as not to discuss the issue of how aggressive they were, because it would be difficult to explain to the Chamber who had the upper hand. Then we have these items which portray us as the side committing crimes over civilians, and then the topic is directed in a different direction while neglecting what the SRK had to go through throughout the war, because they were exceptionally combative and ready to prevail over the SRK, including the population in the area we covered.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On the subject of sniping still - I'm just going in another direction - in your testimony in chief, you talked -- you said at transcript page 32834 that when sniper fire was opened from the other side and you responded either by crossfire or fire opened in one direction, you knew that it would happen that due to fire, bullets would also hit the trams. So did you mean to say that UNPROFOR and the local authorities allowed the trams in Sarajevo to run in unsafe situations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think their intentions were precisely that. As regards the trams, it was confirmed by way of information that the population avoided using them, although of course they had their needs, too. However, they had been provided with a guarantee. They were told that it was the armed forces that were protecting them. In order to protect a tram passing through, they would open fire at our side. But it is not clear to me why they wouldn't realise that we would return fire with fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When opening fire at us, they were not in a position to protect civilians without exposing those civilians to risk.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I take it your answer to my question is yes, that as far as you're concerned, United Nations officials and local authorities allowed the trams in Sarajevo to run in unsafe situations.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not prepared to confirm what the authorities -- or actually the officials of the UN were guided by. I'm simply confirming the practice which took place, and I can confirm that they moved about even when no security was guaranteed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, General, the evidence that's been received by this Chamber says that the practice was the trams were only allowed to run in cease-fires, and that's from the civilians who rode the trams, at T 6766, and the tram drivers themselves at P482, P485, and P495. The people who were riding and driving the trams say that they were only moving at times of cease-fire in direct contradiction, isn't it, to what you've just asserted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't contravene what I said. What somebody had in mind before a tram moved out is something I cannot discuss. Of course, one cannot deny that they thought along the lines of, Well, we're not going to send people out on the trams when there is combat. But at the moment such movement begins and they open fire, it means that they take the responsibility for initiating action. The responsibility is on their side, and they should not initiate their activity at the same time there is tram movement. I don't know whether this is clear or known that the tram lines ran close to their lines of defence where their units were deployed. So they asked for opening fire, and someone else should bear the blame.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: They asked for opening fire, but you've just acknowledged that your forces did open fire on the trams. Isn't that the case? You opened fire and you hit them.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We opened fire on their forces, not on the trams. I did not concede to that. It's not a matter of whether I concede to it or not. That detail alone means nothing. I was discussing the situation and not confessing to something or denying it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, to be completely literal, did your forces fire at the trams or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when you said in your testimony at 32834: "In situations when fire was opened from the other side and then we responded, either crossfire or fire open in one direction. I know that it would happen due to fire, bullets would also hit the trams," what were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If on your side or with anyone else there is no clear idea of what things look like when there is combat, then I can't explain it. In this situation, I'm certain of the fact that it is something that is difficult for you to imagine. You cannot picture what goes on and what kind of fire is exchanged, in what direction and where those bullets fly due to such an effect on the enemy. Not all of the bullets go where they should or where they were aimed at. There is a dispersion with any weapon up to the extent of opening up entirely new topics on the efficiency and direction of bursts of fire from an automatic weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So bullets from your side did hit the trams, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are you insisting on this, that the trams were hit by our bullets? If we put that in a situation where that could have occurred due to other reasons other than the intention of someone hitting the tram, then the assertion that our bullets hit them cannot be placed in terms of blame on our side or on the back of the person who opened fire. I see that you're not prepared to understand that this can happen even when there is no intention on the part of the shooter.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't. I couldn't confirm that we fired at trams. To the contrary, we didn't, and that is why I didn't confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, you said earlier in your answers to me that you didn't exclude the possibility of somebody deranged taking sniping action that had not been approved, and on that note I just want to go over to something that you said in your evidence in chief. You told Dr. Karadzic that over the course of your command of the corps, you had signed and submitted about 70 criminal reports for further procedure, and that's transcript page 32859 to 32860. Now, what kind of offences did you -- were those -- did those reports refer to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I hope that you, as did I, read the document that was offered here. It includes an analysis of what kind of criminal and misdemeanour reports were submitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I just want to know from you if you could give us an idea what kind of offences did you submit reports on. Failing to report for duty, for example?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what it's about. We're not trying to make things relative. We didn't submit criminal reports if someone wore their cap improperly. I was simply trying to get at information -- well, I wasn't trying to say that we initiated proceedings for acts that were irrelevant. We undertook all measures which indicated criminal responsibility of any kind, including violent crime and other types of crime. Of course, I'm not well versed in such terms, and I'd rather not dwell on it too long. And this includes war crimes. I don't know if I have answered sufficiently. In any case, that was the nature of the criminal reports submitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Were any -- was there any one of those criminal reports that related to firing on civilians in Sarajevo in any regard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say if there were such criminal reports. I don't know that. I do know what we prevented and on what topics there were investigations in order to determine any impropriety. I believe you should take into account that what happened and we were unaware of in terms of a result of a certain event due to such activity which had the character, the nature of fighting. It doesn't mean that we necessarily knew that someone was wounded or injured, and if there was information, we initiated proceedings in order to discover the perpetrators. If there was something that happened on the enemy side and we were unaware of it, then --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ah. I was just trying to see if -- I've interrupted you, because I was just trying to look for information of what might have happened on the enemy side. So I apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You just said it doesn't necessarily -- it doesn't mean that we necessarily knew someone was wounded or injured, but if there was information, you initiated proceedings. And then you said, before I interrupted you, "If there was something that happened on the enemy side and we were unaware of it ..." Would you like to finish your sentence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if I didn't complete that, it is well understood. If there's something I don't know, if there's something I'm unaware of, no procedure can be initiated either to praise or discipline.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the subject of these criminal reports that you say you filed, Luka Dragicevic, who you might remember from your trial where he came to testify as a Prosecution witness, came to testify as a Defence witness in your trial, and you remember him. He was your morale, religious, and legal affairs officer from December 1994, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. But he didn't testify as a Defence witness. He was a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Here at the Tribunal. In the Karadzic case he's testified as a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, he was -- he was asked specifically about criminal reports, because, General, you've said you weren't -- couldn't recall whether or not reports had been filed related to allegations of shelling or sniping civilians in Bosnian-held Sarajevo, and here's the question he was asked, and actually, this is what he said in your trial, and that was read out to him at transcript pages 31437 to 31440. In your trial he was asked: "During the time that you were assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs from the beginning of December 1994 until the end of the war, do you recall any instances where a commander from the SRK reported a criminal violation of the international laws of war to the military prosecutor?" And he said: "I never learned or heard of something like that happening in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in the period you referred to. As far as I can remember, if there had been any such thing in these reports from the Prosecutor's office, then certainly officers from the command would have received information about that and taken appropriate measures." And he was asked whether he stood by that answer in this trial, and he said that he did. So, General, I'm a bit puzzled because you said you filed criminal reports on war crimes, and the man whose job it was to deal with these matters now gave evidence in two trials saying that under your command he doesn't recall a single instance of you reporting a criminal violation of international laws of war to the military prosecutor. So it appears that his evidence in two trials directly contradicts what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is your conclusion. I stand by what I believe, and that is that he said accurately what he knew. I'll explain.
